newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa joins regional peacekeeping exercise.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa joins regional peacekeeping exercise.

text.p: South Africa's first international peacekeeping force joins troops from other southern African states in Zimbabwe this week for a combined regional training exercise.
The first of the 1,069 South African peacekeepers leave Bloemspruit base in the central Free State province on Tuesday.
They will train side-by-side troops from seven other countries for three weeks in the first regional peacekeeping effort under the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC).
Fifty-three army vehicles and 110 tonnes of equipment will accompany the South Africans to Nyanga, about 150km (93 miles) east of Zimbabwe's capital Harare.

"It's history in the making because it is the first time that we as the defence force take part in a peacekeeping exercise. This is to enhance regional, and especially southern African liaison," Colonel Kobus Loubser told reporters.
The troops going to Zimbabwe are from one of the two battalions that South Africa has trained for peackeeping over the past two years.
Loubser said they were ready to act as soon as the United Nations issued a call-up.
South Africa has one of the most modern, best equipped and well trained military forces on the African continent, wrought with civil wars and internal conflicts.
"It can happen quickly, as you know. The U.N. can ask us any day to come and help and if we can we will.
"I'm sure we are ready. We have done our training," Loubser said, adding that the training exercise in Zimbabwe was vital to prepare South African soldiers to work with other nations' forces.

The U.N. has said it would send peacekeepers to help end Zaire's civil war if its leaders agree to a ceasefire. This now stands out as the most imminent challenge to a southern African peacekeeping force.
Lieutenant Kallie du Plessis said the South African army adapted to train its troops in frontline peacekeeping.
"It's very different. Normally we are trained for conventional warfare and for so many decades we were trained to be aggressive. Peacekeeping is the complete opposite," he said.

South Africa first tried to launch a National Peacekeeping Force (NPKF) in 1994 to oversee the smooth running of the country's all-race elections, which ended decades of white domination and put the African National Congress (ANC) into power.

But the troubled NPKF, which combined for the first time units of police, regular soldiers, black homeland armies and the armed wing of the ANC, had to be disbanded five months later after internal squabbling and indiscipline.
